newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn coalition at odds over solidarity tax.
newsitem.headline: Bonn coalition at odds over solidarity tax.

text.p: Rudi Geil, Chancellor Helmut Kohl's new commissioner for east German affairs, threatened to spark fresh debate in the coalition over aid to the formerly communist region by opposing the planned solidarity tax cut.

Geil told the Bild am Sonntag newspaper the eastern states would continue to need aid for years to come, and that the planned cut in the solidarity tax, which helps finance such aid, sends the wrong signal.
"It would be best to keep the solidarity tax at its current level," Geil said, adding that the economic upswing in the east is far from self-sustaining.

The economics ministry said Bild am Sonntag quoted Geil incompletely and out of context. Geil did not mean to question the meticulously negotiated coalition compromise, the ministry said in a statement.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel has made a cut in the solidarity tax to 5.5 percent from the current 7.5 percent, effective January 1998, a centrepiece of his planned tax reform aimed at stimulating jobs and investment.
Guido Westerwelle, general secretary of Kohl's junior coalition partners the Free Democrats, said Geil's remarks threatened to reopen the sensitive debate.
Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl and Christian Democrat general secretary Peter Hintze also said the government would stand by its plans.

Paul Krueger, spokesman for the east German CDU parliamentarians, backed Geil and said he too opposed the cut, though he conceded the tax was a burden on the economy that might better be replaced by investment incentives.
Transfers to the east have totaled over one trillion marks since German unification in 1990.
